stories.headline: DOW CROSSES 51,000 FOR FIRST TIME; S&P 500 LOGS NINTH STRAIGHT WINNING WEEK
stories.body: The Dow closed at 51,032 on Friday (+0.72%), crossing 51,000 for the first time in history, while the S&P 500 notched its ninth consecutive weekly gain and seventh straight winning session. Easing geopolitical tensions and resilient corporate earnings continue to underpin the rally.

stories.headline: US-IRAN CEASEFIRE EXTENSION CRUSHES OIL, LIFTS GOLD
stories.body: Reports of a US-Iran ceasefire extension sent WTI crude down 1.9% to $87/barrel — on pace for a 17% monthly decline — while gold surged 2.5% to $4,580/oz. The Strait of Hormuz supply-disruption premium is rapidly unwinding from crude, while gold reflects residual safe-haven demand.

stories.headline: KNICKS REACH NBA FINALS FOR FIRST TIME SINCE 1999; AWAIT THUNDER-SPURS GAME 7
stories.body: New York swept Cleveland 4-0 in the Eastern Conference Finals, with Jalen Brunson earning ECF MVP. The Knicks await the winner of Saturday's Thunder-Spurs Game 7 in the West Finals — the NBA Finals tip off June 3 on ABC.

stories.headline: SEAHAWKS FRANCHISE SALE COULD ECLIPSE $10 BILLION, CLOSE BEFORE 2026 SEASON
stories.body: NFL insider Ian Rapoport reports the market for the Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks has "picked up steam," with a sale potentially exceeding $10B and closing by August. Bidding groups include a Wyc Grousbeck–Aditya Mittal consortium and Sun Microsystems co-founder Vinod Khosla.

stories.headline: WASHINGTON WRAPS SPRING BALL; DEFENSE SHINES IN DAWGS AFTER DARK GAME
stories.body: The Huskies closed spring camp with the Dawgs After Dark spring game at Husky Stadium, Purple beating Gold 27-10 before 10,000–15,000 fans. Defensive players Devin Hyde and Xe'Ree Alexander stood out; Coach Jedd Fisch heads into year three of his tenure.

stories.headline: MICHIGAN'S DUSTY MAY SIGNS FIVE-YEAR EXTENSION AFTER NATIONAL TITLE
stories.body: Coach Dusty May agreed to a five-year deal through 2030-31 after leading Michigan to the 2026 NCAA championship (69-63 over UConn) — the program's first title since 1989. The NCAA also confirmed the men's tournament will expand from 68 to 76 teams in future seasons.

deepDive.title: Geopolitical Risk Premiums in Oil — and Why a Ceasefire Can Move Markets More Than OPEC
content: WTI crude fell nearly 2% Friday to $87/barrel on reports that the US and Iran may extend their ceasefire, putting oil on pace for a 17% monthly decline. That kind of move looks outsized relative to any change in physical barrels — because it's not about physical supply today. It's about the unwinding of a risk premium that markets had embedded for months. Understanding that premium is essential for anyone watching commodities or inflation.

Oil markets price two things simultaneously: current fundamental supply-demand (production, inventories, refinery runs) and an option-like premium for future disruption risk. Iran produces roughly 3–3.5 million barrels per day and controls access to the Strait of Hormuz — the chokepoint through which about 20% of global oil trade passes. Any credible threat to that flow gets priced in immediately, often well before any actual disruption occurs. When the threat recedes, the premium compresses just as fast. Friday's 2% decline reflects the market repricing that probability lower — not a change in what's physically flowing today.

The oil-to-inflation transmission channel is one of the most empirically consistent relationships in macro. Energy directly accounts for roughly 7–8% of the CPI basket, but indirect pass-through — shipping costs, agricultural inputs, industrial energy — roughly doubles that footprint. The 2022 shock illustrated the lag structure clearly: Brent peaked near $130/barrel in March 2022, but headline CPI didn't top out until June 2022 at 9.1%, a roughly three-month lag. The deflationary inverse works too — WTI's decline from $95 to $70 in late 2022 directly enabled the disinflation narrative that markets ran with throughout 2023.

If the Iran ceasefire holds and oil stays compressed below $90 into June and July, the Fed faces a meaningful easing of headline inflation pressure just as it is trying to hold a 'higher for longer' posture. Lower oil feeds into lower headline PCE mechanically within 60–90 days. Watch the June 5 nonfarm payrolls report for the labor-side read, then the June CPI print: if both show moderation alongside subdued energy prices, the combination could accelerate the timeline for rate cuts — or at minimum, make the 'no cuts' narrative increasingly hard for the Fed to defend publicly.
